newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-British inflation dips, rates stay steady.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-British inflation dips, rates stay steady.

text.p: The British government said on Thursday that inflation dipped to 2.5 percent in December from 2.7 percent the previous month, raising expectations for steady interest rates in the run-up to this year's general election.

Minutes after the data were released, the Bank of England signalled that rates were left unchanged at 6.0 percent after Wednesday's regular meeting between finance minister Kenneth Clarke and central bank governor Eddie George.

The government said retail prices rose 0.3 percent last month, after a 0.1 percent rise in November. The figures were at the lower end of analysts' estimates and cooled fears about inflationary pressures in Britain's strong economy.
Financial markets had been braced for a possible hike in rates and the news boosted stock prices and depressed the pound.

"Inflation is moderating, it's coming down. I think it's going to be less than 2.5 percent by the late spring and less than 2.0 percent by the end of the year," said Roger Nightingale of Latinvest Securities.
Excluding mortgage interest payments, the inflation rate fell to 3.1 percent last month from 3.3 percent in November, its first fall since May, the Office for National Statistics said.
"These figures show that subdued cost pressures and a stronger pound are feeding through to lower inflation," Clarke said in a statement after the data were released.

The government is banking that a "feelgood factor" will seep through the economy and help it close a stubborn 20-point lead held by the opposition Labour Party in opinion polls. National parliamentary elections must be held by May 22.

"I will set interest rates at whatever is necessary...my job is to create conditions in which unemployment keeps falling, in which jobs continue to be created and make those jobs more secure. I want living standards to go up," Clarke said before the figures were released.

The government statistics office said the fall in the annual inflation rate was largely due to lower motoring costs and food prices, though there was also help from cheaper leisure goods. The annual rate was driven upwards by higher housing costs and rises in the price of alcohol.
With rates unchanged at the 6.0 percent level reached last October when they rose one quarter of a point, financial traders pushed the British pound slighly lower and stock prices higher.
The FTSE index of leading shares jumped 31 points to 4,189.9 at one point and within a whisker of the record trading high of 4,191.5 set on Wednesday.
